method: One glyph chain over the whole line, fitted on the Currier B paragraph lines of the public practice training pages only (2,042 lines without uncertain readings). Each line is turned into a single string of symbols: its glyphs (the repository's glyph segmentation), a word-space symbol between words, and a line-end symbol after the last word. The only fitted statistic is how often each symbol follows the four symbols before it (fewer at the start of a line). A line is written symbol by symbol from that table, starting fresh at each line, until the line-end symbol is drawn; line length is not fitted separately, it is whatever the chain gives. There is no word list, no position class, no count of words written so far, and no rule that names any glyph or treats the line end differently from any other symbol: a word space and a line end are two outcomes of the same draw. A line holding a four-word run of the manuscript is discarded and redrawn (seed 408, 3,000 lines, 26,981 words). On the practice split, with whole lines kept, the line-final to mid-line ratio of m is 38.9 on this text against 61.6 for the manuscript (threshold 10, within-line shuffle null passed); a second seed gives 36.2, and a three-symbol context gives 28.9. Poured as a token stream the same text gives 0.92 and fails, as R-001 did. What this shows: in the public B pages a word ending in m is followed by the line end far more often than by a word space, and a short-memory writer that merely continues the local glyph pattern reproduces that. It does not explain why the pattern exists.
